1	# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya
2	
3	> Status: draft v3, for owner review · Updated: 2026-11-09
4	> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
5	> what it gives Compliance.
6	
7	## How to read this
8	
9	Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
10	Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
11	auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.
12	
13	| Marker | Meaning |
14	|---|---|
15	| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes or links the official page (a few rows cite vendor blogs, bulletins or example files instead, e.g. R2.4.1b, R6.3.5, R5.5.4). |
16	| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5), or the ⚠️ part of a mixed row. Reasoned, not documented. |
17	| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
18	| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |
19	
20	Nothing here was checked locally (✅): this is a design without access to Papaya's systems.
21	**GĐ-n** = assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4 (owner-confirmed: GĐ-1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11,
22	14; the others are marked "unconfirmed" where used); **S-n** = success criteria
23	(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
24	`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **OD-n** = owner decisions on this draft (both at the end).
25	Earlier owner answers are cited with their source: "research 6.9.4 Q4", "framing Q8", "Options §9 Q2".
26	
27	---
28	
29	## 1. The decision in one page
30	
31	Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
32	of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.
33	
34	**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):
35	
36	1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
37	   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
38	2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
39	   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
40	3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.
41	
42	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
43	|---|---|
44	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
45	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
46	| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
47	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |
48	
49	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
50	
51	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
52	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
53	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
54	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
55	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
56	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
57	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
58	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
59	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
60	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
61	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
62	  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
63	  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
64	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
65	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
66	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
67	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
68	  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
69	  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
70	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
71	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
72	- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
73	  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
74	  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
75	  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
76	  for speed.
77	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
78	  business associate, as the brief implies.
79	
80	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
81	
82	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
83	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
84	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
85	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
86	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.
87	
88	### Roles
89	
90	| Role | Rule |
91	|---|---|
92	| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
93	| Approver | Always an engineer, never an agent (owner rule, OD5). Named in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). |
94	| Incident responder | Engineer who diagnoses and writes the fix or the JIT request. Never the on-call approver of the same shift (OD7). |
95	| On-call approver | Engineer on the on-call schedule, primary + backup, 24/7; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). While on call they only approve: they write no fix and file no JIT request, so the approver is always distinct from the author (OD7). The primary approves; the backup replaces an unavailable primary (OD2). No platform-team membership is required; all engineers follow one agreed approval procedure (OD2). |
96	| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads, or reviews a night-time read the next working day (layer 6). |
97	| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |
98	
99	---
100	
101	## Layer 1 — Identity and access
102	
103	**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
104	written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
105	to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.
106	
107	**On Papaya's stack**
108	
109	- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
110	  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
111	  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
112	  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
113	  holds.
114	- **Process rules** that follow from this:
115	  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
116	    accepted as a process control, D2);
117	  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
118	    research 6.9.4 Q2);
119	  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
120	  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy and training.
121	    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
122	    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
123	    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
124	    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
125	    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
126	- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
127	  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
128	    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Until a service's logs are redacted at source
129	    (layer 6), it gets that service's metrics only. Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
130	    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
131	    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
132	    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
133	  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
134	  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7), via a partner product, the
135	    TEAM sample (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b) or a small home-built flow (⚠️ R2.4.2) on the documented APIs
136	    `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2);
137	  - no standing prod-write permission set.
138	- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
139	  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
140	    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
141	    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
142	  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
143	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
144	    JIT roles. This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
145	    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
146	  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); protect the org trail (📖 R2.6.2).
147	  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
148	    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path).
149	- **Sessions/MFA:** portal session length set on purpose; an IdP session can extend it silently
150	  (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
151	- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod role trusts only the `production`
152	  environment of the monorepo, in its `sub` format (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4; immutable format assumed,
153	  ⚠️ R3.7 A2), ideally customised with the deploy workflow's `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
154	- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization, which Google
155	  requires (📖 R3.4.5b).
156	- **k0s, GCP and Firebase for humans:** same principles; mechanisms not researched (G1–G3). Today
157	  k0s is reached with kubeconfigs, no SSO (GĐ-4, unconfirmed). Interim: no admin kubeconfig and no GCP
158	  owner role on laptops; prod deploys only from CI. Firebase is not on the GCP BAA list (📖 R5.5.3), so
159	  Firebase Hosting must hold no PHI (⚠️ R5.7 #7).
160	
161	**Audit evidence.** Identity Center assignment export (S1); CloudTrail `CreateAccountAssignment` /
162	`DeleteAccountAssignment` per grant (📖 R2.4.2), linked to its approval by request ID [design]; SCPs
163	and trust policies as Pulumi code; IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on policy PRs
164	(📖 R2.8.1); quarterly access review of permission sets and GitHub admins.
165	
166	**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write and keep a free non-prod loop. Prod reads stay
167	fast for metrics and metadata, but shrink during the transition: because the engineer's access is the
168	agent's access, from phase 1 the engineer too loses raw logs and configuration of services not yet
169	redacted or moved to runtime secrets. Configuration values come from the IaC code instead (layer 1
170	above); raw logs that may hold customer data need an L3-data grant. The data owner is not on the
171	on-call schedule, so at night the grant is approved by the on-call approver alone and the data owner
172	reviews it the next working day [design]; the wait still counts against S7. This is
173	the largest cost of the first months. Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced.
174	
175	---
176	
177	## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls
178	
179	**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
180	and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
181	untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).
182	
183	**On Papaya's stack**
184	
185	- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
186	  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
187	  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
188	- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited. Only the phase-1 subset in layer 8 ships first; the other keys (sandbox, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, credential denies, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowedProviders`) arrive in phase 2 (OD4):
189	
190	  | Key | Value and reason |
191	  |---|---|
192	  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual). A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto; VS Code remembers the last pick (D1, R6.9.3). |
193	  | `permissions.allow` | Read-only commands Papaya uses, to cut prompts (R6.9.3). It contains no command listed in `sandbox.excludedCommands` (`aws`, `pulumi`, `serverless`): an allowed excluded command would run outside the sandbox, with `~/.aws` and the network, without a prompt (⚠️ inference from R1.2.6, R1.6.4) [design]. Cost: a prompt for every `aws` read. |
194	  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true`, one rule set (D1, research 6.9.4 Q4; R1.2.5). Cost: project and user rules are ignored, so the managed set must carry every deny/ask rule projects need; prompts likely rise (⚠️ research 6.9.4 Q4). |
195	  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"`: removes bypass mode (P3a; R1.2.2). Auto mode, where a classifier approves instead of a person, stays available (D1) and is measured through `permission_mode`. |
196	  | `permissions.deny` / `ask` | Deny credential paths (R5.5.4; `Read(...)` syntax ⚠️ R1.8 #5). Ask for `WebFetch`, which the sandbox domain list does not limit (R1.6.2); cost: a prompt per fetch. The HIPAA template denies WebFetch (R5.5.4); "ask" is a deliberate deviation so that documentation lookups still work. |
197	  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ 2.1.285 for `allowedProviders` (R1.1.15), which also covers `--restricted` (2.1.248, R6.9.1b) and the plugin-pin fix (2.1.179, R6.2.7); ≥ 2.1.295 if any managed hook uses `onFailure: "block"` (R1.5.2); and ≥ the latest fixed advisory at rollout (R6.3.9). It does not end running sessions and fails open on a bad value (R1.1.13). |
198	  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org; closes most bypasses on **endpoint-managed** machines (R1.1.15). `forceLoginOrgUUID` checks claude.ai sign-ins only, not Claude Console sign-ins (R5.5.5); with it set, sessions on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or `apiKeyHelper` are refused (R1.11.3.11). |
199	  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` (R1.5.4). |
200	  | sandbox | `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` locked by `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly`; `credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws`, which the sandbox can otherwise read (R1.6.3, R1.6.4). |
201	  | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` | Agent's choice, to confirm (OQ-C) [design]: left at its default `true`. This widens D1's "Manual + read-only allowlist": every sandboxed command, writes in the working directory and calls to allowed domains included, runs without a prompt. Detail: sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, so in Manual mode prompts are for edits, unsandboxed commands and fetches, not every command (R5.5.5b). A deliberate choice: the sandbox (no `~/.aws`, allowlisted network) is the control for those commands. The HIPAA README says to set `false` if policy needs a person to approve each command (R5.5.5b); cost of `false`: a prompt per command. |
202	  | MCP, plugins | Layer 4. |
203	  | OTel | Exporter on, content flags `0` (R1.1.20, R5.5.4). |
204	
205	- **Trade-off on AWS credentials [design].** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, the plan is to
206	  list `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
207	  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), which likely includes the network (⚠️ inference). How the list matches
208	  commands (prefix or text, and chained commands) is not researched (⚠️). This is worse than an
209	  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and
210	  plugins, all code in the repo that the agent can edit, so excluding them lets repo code run
211	  outside the sandbox with network access and with `~/.aws` readable (⚠️ inference). For these
212	  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
213	  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
214	  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
215	  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end
216	  the existing portal session and sign in fresh **before** a JIT or data-read grant is created
217	  (whether ending a session invalidates a token already stolen is unverified ⚠️; ending it does not
218	  end role sessions, 📖 R2.4.3); an SCP that denies writes to resources outside Papaya's organization using
219	  `aws:ResourceOrgID` (key 📖 R2.3.8), on every OU, since the token can be stolen from a non-prod
220	  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
221	  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
222	  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
223	  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
224	  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
225	  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
226	  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
227	  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
228	  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).
229	- **Session types:**
230	
231	  | Session | Identity | Flags | Enforcement |
232	  |---|---|---|---|
233	  | Daily development (laptop) | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | baseline | Auto mode by choice (D1); `--restricted` recommended (D3). |
234	  | Incident analysis (laptop) | meant to be `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"`, started in an empty scratch directory, not the repo [design] | Process rule (D3, research 6.9.4 Q1–Q2). No WebFetch, and file tools confined to the working directory (📖 R6.9.1b); Edit/Write are excluded only if `--tools` acts as an exclusive list (⚠️ unverified), but Bash can still write in its working directory (📖 R1.6.3) and call any role in the cache. |
235	  | CI agent (hosted runner) | own GitHub App token; never `production` | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`; all rules in a managed-settings file on the runner | Workflow file under CODEOWNERS (D3, research 6.9.4 Q5). The file is advisory if `Bash` is in `--tools` (layer 5). |
236	  | JIT terminal | JIT grant | no agent | Process rule (D2). |
237	  | Auto-mode environment (phase 3) | non-prod only | auto encouraged | D1 option (c). |
238	
239	- **Phase-1 interim posture:** the sandbox and credential denies arrive in phase 2 (OD4), so for
240	  the first 30–60 days `~/.aws` is readable and the network is open to every Bash command; in auto
241	  mode the classifier is the only gate. Impact is bounded because standing prod write is removed in
242	  phase 1 (layer 1), but token theft is easier in this window.
243	- **Hard limits:** Bash rules are not a boundary (📖 R1.2.6); hooks fail open unless

267	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
268	
269	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
270	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
271	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. Every prod change needs two people, and
272	no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it (until OQ-A is answered, the
273	cross-team process rule below can need more); the on-call backup only replaces an
274	unavailable primary (OD2). Higher risk narrows **who** may approve (the owners of that path), not how
275	many. Separately, any prod diff that looks risky stops the deploy, whatever its level; that adds a
276	second approval by an owner of the same stack, which keeps it to two people (OD8). Agent's reading
277	of OD8 [design], to confirm: the original author opens the approval PR and the first approver
278	approves it; if the first approver is unavailable, another owner of the stack approves, which makes
279	three people (open question OQ-B). Two edge cases: GitHub accepts one on-call group member for
280	files of several owner teams (OD9, 📖 R3.2.7), so "an approval from each domain team" on a
281	cross-team PR is a process rule only, and an interim default of the agent [design] until OQ-A; whether such PRs should be split is an open question for the
282	owner (OQ-A, below). A real-data read is not a change and has its own rule, L3-data. Incidents use the same
283	path with faster people, not fewer security checks.
284	
285	| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
286	|---|---|---|---|---|
287	| **L0** | Read: non-prod anything; prod metadata | metrics, redacted logs | none | read-only identity |
288	| **L1** | Change in non-prod | deploy a branch to dev; `pulumi preview` on non-prod (needs state-write permission on a DIY S3 backend, 📖 R4.3.3) | author only | non-prod roles or PR pipeline |
289	| **L2** | Routine prod change in code | Lambda timeout/memory, ECS desired count, release | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher | PR → `main` → deploy workflow |
290	| **L3** | High-risk prod change | IAM/SCP; replace/delete of stateful resources; network; `.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/**`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`, `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, plugin/MCP catalogue; advisory policy finding | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher. L3 paths (workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, stacks that hold only IAM/SCP): the L3 owner team. L3 content inside a domain file (an IAM statement in `serverless.yml`, a stateful delete): the stack's owner, then the risk stop (OD8). In incidents: the on-call approver for deployable paths (OD9); paths that define the process (CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, workflows) wait for the L3 owner team | same path; for IaC changes the risk stop also applies; workflow and agent-config files have no prod diff |
291	| **L3-JIT** | Break-glass | ECS force-redeploy while Actions is down | on-call approver ≠ requester (Options §4b); agent's reading of OD9: the on-call approver counts as owner of the service in the request [design] | layer 7 |
292	| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |
293	
294	`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for
295	the whole team (OD3). With code-owner review on, every PR, L2 included, needs an approval from an
296	owner of the files it touches (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7; per-file behaviour ⚠️ not a separate research row).
297	What differs at L3 is **which team** owns the path: L3 paths are owned in CODEOWNERS by a designated
298	L3 owner team (deployable L3 paths also by the on-call group, OD9), L2 paths by their domain team; and IaC changes at L3 meet the
299	risk stop. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files, so they are approved by
300	the stack's owners, not the L3 team (OD8); automated checks make up for this: IAM Access Analyzer
301	`check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and the Pulumi policy pack (📖 R4.2.2), both from phase 2 (layer 5). Cost: changes to `CLAUDE.md` (where D3 puts shared knowledge) need the L3 owner team, not
302	the domain team that edits it most.
303	
304	**On Papaya's stack**
305	
306	- **Gate = merge to `main`.** On Team, environment reviewers do not exist for private repos
307	  (📖 R3.1.2). Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
308	  approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
309	  push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). Branch up to date before merge, since there is
310	  no merge queue (⚠️ R4.6 #1; whether updating drops approvals is open, Options §8).
311	- **L3 approvals [design]:** CODEOWNERS plus code-owner review only, no path-based required
312	  reviewers rule. That rule (📖 R3.2.4) asks for approvals from specific teams, which the on-call
313	  group would not satisfy at night, and how it combines several teams is not researched (⚠️), so it
314	  would break OD9 or add a third person. GitHub stops the author from approving (📖 R3.3.1). A required check with a pinned source app (📖 R3.2.5), computed by a dedicated GitHub App or by a workflow that runs from the base branch, not from PR code [design], adds what
315	  the rules cannot: for app-opened PRs it excludes the person who triggered the agent, and it counts
316	  only human approvals, since an app's approval might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3).
317	- **Who approves at night (OD9):** a fixed GitHub team, the on-call approvers, is listed as
318	  co-owner on every deployable path in CODEOWNERS (infrastructure and service code), next to the
319	  domain team. Agent's reading of OD9, to confirm: the group does **not** co-own the paths that
320	  define the process (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md` and agent config, catalogue); those stay
321	  with the L3 owner team only. If a broken workflow blocks a night fix, the pipeline counts as
322	  unavailable and the JIT fallback applies (layer 7). One primary and one backup from that team are on call. Technically any member can approve any
323	  path; by rule the primary approves and the backup only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
324	  Membership is fixed, not changed per shift [design]. GitHub team membership is set in organization
325	  settings, not by a PR; managing it as code (e.g. with Pulumi's GitHub provider) and the audit
326	  event for a membership change are not researched (⚠️ G16). Meanwhile the layer-7 settings
327	  comparison includes the group's member list. Cost: an approval from any
328	  listed owner satisfies code-owner review (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days a member could approve
329	  another domain's PR, on or off shift. Mitigation [design]: process rule "approve another
330	  domain's PR only if it carries the `incident` label and you are on shift", and a monthly report of
331	  every cross-domain approval by group members on PRs without that label (layer 7). Whether Papaya's team size allows full coverage is unknown
332	  (§1, S7).
333	- **Risk stop [design]:** applies to every deploy, whatever the level. The deploy job previews prod;
334	  on stateful replace/delete, an IAM change, a network or security-group change, or an advisory
335	  policy finding it stops and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a second PR that adds
336	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` (`<sha>` = the stopped commit) holding that SHA and the
337	  preview hash; the workflow does not open it, because the setting that lets Actions create and approve PRs stays
338	  off (📖 R3.3.3; ⚠️ R3.6 #3). CODEOWNERS on `deploy-approvals/<stack>/` names the owners of that stack and the
339	  on-call group (OD8, OD9). The approver is ≠ author and may be the first PR's approver, who now sees
340	  the prod diff. Merging it triggers the deploy on the new HEAD, which previews again and continues
341	  only if the hash matches the approved one; if another PR merged in between, the hash differs and
342	  the deploy stops again (Options §1; hash stability ⚠️ Options §8). Cost: while a stack is
343	  stopped, later merges to that stack stop too until a matching approval lands; in an incident, a
344	  risky change already waiting on `main` blocks the fix for the same stack until it is approved or
345	  reverted. A
346	  `mandatory` policy violation always blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2): the fix is a code change, or a
347	  change to the policy pack through its own L3 PR. Preview output is filtered for
348	  outputs and secrets before it is posted (Options §1; ⚠️ R4.6 #2).
349	- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if (⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c): `production`
350	  allows only `main`; only the reusable deploy workflow (under CODEOWNERS) references it; no ref/SHA
351	  inputs; no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers; one concurrency group
352	  per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4).
353	- **Pulumi:** PRs preview non-prod only, because a prod preview runs PR code with state-write and
354	  secret access (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). On `main`: prod preview, then `pulumi up` with the
355	  policy pack, which stops on a mandatory violation (📖 R4.2.2). Prod runs allow no `--skip-preview`
356	  (📖 R4.1.2) and no targeting, replace, `state`, `import`, `destroy` (⚠️ R4.6 #3, G12). Pulumi Cloud,
357	  if used: OIDC via `pulumi/auth-actions`, no stored token (📖 R4.1.4).
358	- **Serverless v4:** `serverless package`; `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0), parsed by CI
359	  because differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2); `serverless deploy --package`
360	  (📖 R4.4.3); a least-privilege `deploymentRole`, which cannot be removed later and is usable by
361	  anyone who may operate the stack (📖 R4.4.5), so JIT roles get no stack-operation rights.
362	- **State:** writable by deploy roles (and possibly the drift role, layer 7); Pulumi
363	  secrets via `awskms` on a DIY backend (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #7).
364	- **k0s [design]:** manifests in the monorepo, applied by CI; no write RBAC for humans or agents in
365	  prod; read roles exclude logs and exec in namespaces with claim data (mechanism: G1). The risk
366	  stop is described for Pulumi and Serverless only; for k0s manifests (RBAC changes are the IAM
367	  equivalent) a `kubectl diff`-based stop is a candidate, not researched (⚠️ G1). Firebase deploys
368	  have no preview step in this design (⚠️ G2).
369	- **Incident lane:** label `incident`, on-call approver paged, security checks always run (S10), only
370	  slow unrelated tests skipped [design].
371	
372	**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)
373	
374	The incident responder is engineer E; the on-call approver is R (a backup replaces R only if R is
375	unavailable).
376	
377	1. E's incident-analysis session reads metrics and redacted logs and proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s,
378	   memory 1024 → 2048 MB, and a larger visibility timeout on the source queue (ratio ⚠️ Options §8).
379	2. A second session (edit tools; not meant to use prod roles) edits `serverless.yml`, runs
380	   `serverless diff` on non-prod, and opens a PR labelled `incident` as E.
381	3. R, a co-owner of `serverless.yml` through the on-call group (OD9), reviews the diff. If R
382	   catches a missing queue change, R does not fix it (OD7): E pushes the fix, the stale approval is
383	   dismissed, and R approves again, one more review round (Options §6). E merges.
384	4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, finds no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
385	5. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6) against ≤ 30 min: measured first in rollout.
386	
387	**Audit evidence.** The PR (diff, approvers, checks); run log and preview artifact, exported because
388	retention is unverified (⚠️ G7); deploy-role CloudTrail events; all linked by commit SHA and run ID.
389	
390	**Cost / value.** One approver for every prod change, from the owners of the path; two approvals by
391	the same approver when the risk stop fires. Cross-team PRs: open (OQ-A). None in non-prod.
392	Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub. Gap: on Team the prod diff is not seen before apply.

433	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
434	
435	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
436	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
437	checks as human code (S10).
438	
439	**On Papaya's stack**
440	
441	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
442	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
443	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
444	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
445	  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
446	  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
447	  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
448	  - stored only as an **environment secret of `production`**, never as a repository secret. Anyone
449	    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
450	    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
451	    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
452	    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
453	  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
454	    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be
455	    treated like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5). Self-hosted runners "can be persistently
456	    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which
457	    repositories use them (📖 R3.5.2); in a monorepo any workflow can likely target the runner's label (⚠️ G15).
458	    How to restrict a runner to one workflow is not researched (⚠️ G15); just-in-time runners exist
459	    (📖 R3.5.2, not read in detail). If reaching k0s needs a self-hosted runner, that
460	    runner is dedicated to the `production` deploy, and the residual risk is recorded;
461	  - that environment secret is the single source of truth: no copy elsewhere (OD1);
462	  - an owner, an expiry and rotation in the exception register;
463	  - optionally a separate environment (e.g. `production-k0s`), limited to `main` and referenced
464	    only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read these secrets
465	    [design].
466	
467	  Residual risk: admins can change the environment, and a deleted environment comes back without
468	  protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); the alerts and settings comparison in layer 7 cover this. The exception
469	  covers **CI deploy credentials only**. Runtime credentials, such as a k0s autoscaler's AWS access to
470	  add or remove nodes, live in the cluster, not in GitHub; they follow layer 1 (no static keys, a
471	  role attached to the machine; ⚠️ not researched for k0s, G1).
472	- **Side paths:** Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard providers reach AWS
473	  (📖 R4.4.9) outside the GitHub gate (⚠️ R4.4.9); not used for prod (⚠️ R4.6 #6).
474	- **Pinning:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org policy "Require
475	  actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" (availability on Team ⚠️); the lockfile does not pin reusable workflows, so
476	  the deploy workflow lives in the same repo (📖 R3.5.5; conclusion [design]).
477	- **CODEOWNERS** on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`,
478	  `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc` (📖 R3.2.8; list ⚠️ R6.5 #5); CI validates the file, because
479	  invalid lines are skipped silently (📖 R3.2.7).
480	- **No privileged triggers with untrusted code** (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` + checkout,
481	  📖 R3.5.4).
482	- **Agents in CI:** `claude-code-action` with a custom GitHub App limited to Contents, Issues, Pull
483	  requests (📖 R1.7.8); Anthropic workload identity federation, not a personal OAuth token (📖 R1.7.6);
484	  `--restricted` and explicit `--tools` (D3; passing it through `claude_args` unverified, ⚠️ research
485	  6.9.4 Q5); a managed-settings file on the runner, which also guards against mods (📖 R1.5.6; for
486	  federation auth ⚠️); MCP set fixed by CI because `.mcp.json` loads without a prompt in `-p` runs
487	  (📖 R1.3.5); never `environment: production` (⚠️ R3.6 #4). Hosted runners give `sudo` (📖 R3.5.1),

509	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
510	
511	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
512	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
513	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
514	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
515	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
516	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
517	
518	**On Papaya's stack**
519	
520	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
521	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
522	    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
523	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
524	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
525	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
526	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
527	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
528	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
529	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
530	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
531	  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
532	  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
533	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
534	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
535	    redacted summary. This
536	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
537	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
538	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
539	    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
540	    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
541	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
542	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
543	  1.11.4 L6).
544	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
545	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
546	  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path
547	  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
548	  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
549	  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
550	  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
551	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
552	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
553	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
554	  (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).
555	- **Non-prod:** no prod copies (S11). A scan of non-prod stores runs at the start of phase 1 (tool:
556	  G4); a store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule (GĐ-14: until cleaned, non-prod follows the GĐ-9 data-read rule). Cost: until scanned, that store is
557	  not part of the free loop.
558	- **Local stores:** transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (research 1.11.4); set
559	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).
560	- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** processing data collected in Vietnam on a platform abroad is a
561	  transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts, update the
562	  transfer impact assessment (⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).
563	
564	**Audit evidence.** SCP/IAM text as the written access rule for sensitive data (📖 R5.4.3; ⚠️ R5.7 #5);
565	data-read requests and the data-read role's CloudTrail; planted-injection reports (layer 8); non-prod
566	scan results (S11).
567	
568	**Cost / value.** Debugging with redacted and synthetic data; a request for the rare real-data read.
569	Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores (fully from phase 2;
570	actions ⚠️ G13) and by process
571	elsewhere, and a record per exception (S9).
572	
573	---
574	
575	## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass
576	
577	**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
578	named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
579	is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.
580	
581	**On Papaya's stack**
582	
583	- **Audit stores:**
584	  - organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account with integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4,
585	    R2.6.5); change records ≥ 6 years; raw-log retention for Papaya's compliance owner (⚠️ R5.7 #2).
586	    Data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and prod SQS (cost 📖 R2.6.3; selection
587	    ⚠️ R2.9 #5), which makes the archive
588	    PHI-bearing (⚠️ research 1.11.4 L15). CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers (📖 R2.6.6);
589	  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days, so exported (📖 R3.5.6);
590	  - alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`,

592	    (📖 R3.5.6, R3.1.4; selection ⚠️ R3.6 #1). UI changes to the branch policy may leave no event, and a
593	    deleted `production` environment comes back unprotected (⚠️ R3.1.4): a job compares live settings
594	    with an expected copy (G8);
595	  - Aurora SQL is likely invisible to CloudTrail (⚠️ R2.7.1): Database Activity Streams, alerts on
596	    lost-record events (📖 R2.7.2; Serverless v2 ⚠️), stream treated as PHI (⚠️ R2.7.3);
597	  - Claude Code OTel without prompt content (layer 2).

1	# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya
2	
3	> Status: draft v3, for owner review · Updated: 2026-11-09
4	> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
5	> what it gives Compliance.
6	
7	## How to read this
8	
9	Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
10	Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
11	auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.
12	
13	| Marker | Meaning |
14	|---|---|
15	| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes or links the official page (a few rows cite vendor blogs, bulletins or example files instead, e.g. R2.4.1b, R6.3.5, R5.5.4). |
16	| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5), or the ⚠️ part of a mixed row. Reasoned, not documented. |
17	| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
18	| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |
19	
20	Nothing here was checked locally (✅): this is a design without access to Papaya's systems.
21	**GĐ-n** = assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4 (owner-confirmed: GĐ-1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11,
22	14; the others are marked "unconfirmed" where used); **S-n** = success criteria
23	(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
24	`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **OD-n** = owner decisions on this draft (both at the end).
25	Earlier owner answers are cited with their source: "research 6.9.4 Q4", "framing Q8", "Options §9 Q2".
26	
27	---
28	
29	## 1. The decision in one page
30	
31	Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
32	of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.
33	
34	**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):
35	
36	1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
37	   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
38	2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
39	   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
40	3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.
41	
42	| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
43	|---|---|
44	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
45	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
46	| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
47	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |
48	
49	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
50	
51	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
52	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
53	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
54	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
55	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
56	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
57	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
58	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
59	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
60	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
61	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
62	  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
63	  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
64	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
65	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
66	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
67	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
68	  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
69	  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
70	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
71	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
72	- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
73	  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
74	  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
75	  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
76	  for speed.
77	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
78	  business associate, as the brief implies.
79	
80	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
81	
82	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
83	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
84	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
85	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
86	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.

88	### Roles
89	
90	| Role | Rule |
91	|---|---|
92	| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
93	| Approver | Always an engineer, never an agent (owner rule, OD5). Named in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). |
94	| Incident responder | Engineer who diagnoses and writes the fix or the JIT request. Never the on-call approver of the same shift (OD7). |
95	| On-call approver | Engineer on the on-call schedule, primary + backup, 24/7; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). While on call they only approve: they write no fix and file no JIT request, so the approver is always distinct from the author (OD7). The primary approves; the backup replaces an unavailable primary (OD2). No platform-team membership is required; all engineers follow one agreed approval procedure (OD2). |
96	| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads, or reviews a night-time read the next working day (layer 6). |
97	| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |

101	## Layer 1 — Identity and access
102	
103	**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
104	written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
105	to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.
106	
107	**On Papaya's stack**
108	
109	- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
110	  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
111	  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
112	  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
113	  holds.
114	- **Process rules** that follow from this:
115	  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
116	    accepted as a process control, D2);
117	  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
118	    research 6.9.4 Q2);
119	  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
120	  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy and training.
121	    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
122	    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
123	    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
124	    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
125	    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
126	- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
127	  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
128	    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Until a service's logs are redacted at source
129	    (layer 6), it gets that service's metrics only. Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
130	    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
131	    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
132	    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
133	  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
134	  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7), via a partner product, the
135	    TEAM sample (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b) or a small home-built flow (⚠️ R2.4.2) on the documented APIs
136	    `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2);
137	  - no standing prod-write permission set.
138	- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
139	  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
140	    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
141	    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
142	  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
143	    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
144	    JIT roles. This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
145	    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
146	  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); protect the org trail (📖 R2.6.2).
147	  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
148	    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path).
149	- **Sessions/MFA:** portal session length set on purpose; an IdP session can extend it silently
150	  (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
151	- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod role trusts only the `production`
152	  environment of the monorepo, in its `sub` format (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4; immutable format assumed,
153	  ⚠️ R3.7 A2), ideally customised with the deploy workflow's `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
154	- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization, which Google
155	  requires (📖 R3.4.5b).
156	- **k0s, GCP and Firebase for humans:** same principles; mechanisms not researched (G1–G3). Today
157	  k0s is reached with kubeconfigs, no SSO (GĐ-4, unconfirmed). Interim: no admin kubeconfig and no GCP
158	  owner role on laptops; prod deploys only from CI. Firebase is not on the GCP BAA list (📖 R5.5.3), so
159	  Firebase Hosting must hold no PHI (⚠️ R5.7 #7).
160	
161	**Audit evidence.** Identity Center assignment export (S1); CloudTrail `CreateAccountAssignment` /
162	`DeleteAccountAssignment` per grant (📖 R2.4.2), linked to its approval by request ID [design]; SCPs
163	and trust policies as Pulumi code; IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` on policy PRs
164	(📖 R2.8.1); quarterly access review of permission sets and GitHub admins.
165	
166	**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write and keep a free non-prod loop. Prod reads stay
167	fast for metrics and metadata, but shrink during the transition: because the engineer's access is the
168	agent's access, from phase 1 the engineer too loses raw logs and configuration of services not yet
169	redacted or moved to runtime secrets. Configuration values come from the IaC code instead (layer 1
170	above); raw logs that may hold customer data need an L3-data grant. The data owner is not on the
171	on-call schedule, so at night the grant is approved by the on-call approver alone and the data owner
172	reviews it the next working day [design]; the wait still counts against S7. This is
173	the largest cost of the first months. Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced.

177	## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls
178	
179	**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
180	and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
181	untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).

183	**On Papaya's stack**
184	
185	- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
186	  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
187	  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
188	- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited. Only the phase-1 subset in layer 8 ships first; the other keys (sandbox, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, credential denies, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowedProviders`) arrive in phase 2 (OD4):

206	  list `aws`, `pulumi` and `serverless` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
207	  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), which likely includes the network (⚠️ inference). How the list matches

209	  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and

212	  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
213	  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
214	  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
215	  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end

220	  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
221	  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
222	  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
223	  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
224	  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
225	  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
226	  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
227	  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
228	  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).

267	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
268	
269	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
270	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
271	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. Every prod change needs two people, and
272	no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it (until OQ-A is answered, the
273	cross-team process rule below can need more); the on-call backup only replaces an
274	unavailable primary (OD2). Higher risk narrows **who** may approve (the owners of that path), not how
275	many. Separately, any prod diff that looks risky stops the deploy, whatever its level; that adds a
276	second approval by an owner of the same stack, which keeps it to two people (OD8). Agent's reading
277	of OD8 [design], to confirm: the original author opens the approval PR and the first approver
278	approves it; if the first approver is unavailable, another owner of the stack approves, which makes
279	three people (open question OQ-B). Two edge cases: GitHub accepts one on-call group member for
280	files of several owner teams (OD9, 📖 R3.2.7), so "an approval from each domain team" on a
281	cross-team PR is a process rule only, and an interim default of the agent [design] until OQ-A; whether such PRs should be split is an open question for the
282	owner (OQ-A, below). A real-data read is not a change and has its own rule, L3-data. Incidents use the same
283	path with faster people, not fewer security checks.
284	
285	| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
286	|---|---|---|---|---|
287	| **L0** | Read: non-prod anything; prod metadata | metrics, redacted logs | none | read-only identity |
288	| **L1** | Change in non-prod | deploy a branch to dev; `pulumi preview` on non-prod (needs state-write permission on a DIY S3 backend, 📖 R4.3.3) | author only | non-prod roles or PR pipeline |
289	| **L2** | Routine prod change in code | Lambda timeout/memory, ECS desired count, release | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher | PR → `main` → deploy workflow |
290	| **L3** | High-risk prod change | IAM/SCP; replace/delete of stateful resources; network; `.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/**`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`, `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, plugin/MCP catalogue; advisory policy finding | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher. L3 paths (workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, stacks that hold only IAM/SCP): the L3 owner team. L3 content inside a domain file (an IAM statement in `serverless.yml`, a stateful delete): the stack's owner, then the risk stop (OD8). In incidents: the on-call approver for deployable paths (OD9); paths that define the process (CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, workflows) wait for the L3 owner team | same path; for IaC changes the risk stop also applies; workflow and agent-config files have no prod diff |
291	| **L3-JIT** | Break-glass | ECS force-redeploy while Actions is down | on-call approver ≠ requester (Options §4b); agent's reading of OD9: the on-call approver counts as owner of the service in the request [design] | layer 7 |
292	| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |
293	
294	`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for
295	the whole team (OD3). With code-owner review on, every PR, L2 included, needs an approval from an
296	owner of the files it touches (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7; per-file behaviour ⚠️ not a separate research row).
297	What differs at L3 is **which team** owns the path: L3 paths are owned in CODEOWNERS by a designated
298	L3 owner team (deployable L3 paths also by the on-call group, OD9), L2 paths by their domain team; and IaC changes at L3 meet the
299	risk stop. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files, so they are approved by
300	the stack's owners, not the L3 team (OD8); automated checks make up for this: IAM Access Analyzer
301	`check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and the Pulumi policy pack (📖 R4.2.2), both from phase 2 (layer 5). Cost: changes to `CLAUDE.md` (where D3 puts shared knowledge) need the L3 owner team, not
302	the domain team that edits it most.
303	
304	**On Papaya's stack**
305	
306	- **Gate = merge to `main`.** On Team, environment reviewers do not exist for private repos
307	  (📖 R3.1.2). Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
308	  approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
309	  push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). Branch up to date before merge, since there is
310	  no merge queue (⚠️ R4.6 #1; whether updating drops approvals is open, Options §8).
311	- **L3 approvals [design]:** CODEOWNERS plus code-owner review only, no path-based required
312	  reviewers rule. That rule (📖 R3.2.4) asks for approvals from specific teams, which the on-call
313	  group would not satisfy at night, and how it combines several teams is not researched (⚠️), so it
314	  would break OD9 or add a third person. GitHub stops the author from approving (📖 R3.3.1). A required check with a pinned source app (📖 R3.2.5), computed by a dedicated GitHub App or by a workflow that runs from the base branch, not from PR code [design], adds what
315	  the rules cannot: for app-opened PRs it excludes the person who triggered the agent, and it counts
316	  only human approvals, since an app's approval might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3).
317	- **Who approves at night (OD9):** a fixed GitHub team, the on-call approvers, is listed as
318	  co-owner on every deployable path in CODEOWNERS (infrastructure and service code), next to the
319	  domain team. Agent's reading of OD9, to confirm: the group does **not** co-own the paths that
320	  define the process (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS, `CLAUDE.md` and agent config, catalogue); those stay
321	  with the L3 owner team only. If a broken workflow blocks a night fix, the pipeline counts as
322	  unavailable and the JIT fallback applies (layer 7). One primary and one backup from that team are on call. Technically any member can approve any
323	  path; by rule the primary approves and the backup only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
324	  Membership is fixed, not changed per shift [design]. GitHub team membership is set in organization
325	  settings, not by a PR; managing it as code (e.g. with Pulumi's GitHub provider) and the audit
326	  event for a membership change are not researched (⚠️ G16). Meanwhile the layer-7 settings
327	  comparison includes the group's member list. Cost: an approval from any
328	  listed owner satisfies code-owner review (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days a member could approve
329	  another domain's PR, on or off shift. Mitigation [design]: process rule "approve another
330	  domain's PR only if it carries the `incident` label and you are on shift", and a monthly report of
331	  every cross-domain approval by group members on PRs without that label (layer 7). Whether Papaya's team size allows full coverage is unknown
332	  (§1, S7).
333	- **Risk stop [design]:** applies to every deploy, whatever the level. The deploy job previews prod;
334	  on stateful replace/delete, an IAM change, a network or security-group change, or an advisory
335	  policy finding it stops and posts the filtered preview. The original author opens a second PR that adds
336	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<sha>.yaml` (`<sha>` = the stopped commit) holding that SHA and the
337	  preview hash; the workflow does not open it, because the setting that lets Actions create and approve PRs stays
338	  off (📖 R3.3.3; ⚠️ R3.6 #3). CODEOWNERS on `deploy-approvals/<stack>/` names the owners of that stack and the
339	  on-call group (OD8, OD9). The approver is ≠ author and may be the first PR's approver, who now sees
340	  the prod diff. Merging it triggers the deploy on the new HEAD, which previews again and continues
341	  only if the hash matches the approved one; if another PR merged in between, the hash differs and
342	  the deploy stops again (Options §1; hash stability ⚠️ Options §8). Cost: while a stack is
343	  stopped, later merges to that stack stop too until a matching approval lands; in an incident, a
344	  risky change already waiting on `main` blocks the fix for the same stack until it is approved or
345	  reverted. A
346	  `mandatory` policy violation always blocks `pulumi up` (📖 R4.2.2): the fix is a code change, or a
347	  change to the policy pack through its own L3 PR. Preview output is filtered for
348	  outputs and secrets before it is posted (Options §1; ⚠️ R4.6 #2).
349	- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if (⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c): `production`
350	  allows only `main`; only the reusable deploy workflow (under CODEOWNERS) references it; no ref/SHA
351	  inputs; no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers; one concurrency group
352	  per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4).
353	- **Pulumi:** PRs preview non-prod only, because a prod preview runs PR code with state-write and
354	  secret access (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #2). On `main`: prod preview, then `pulumi up` with the
355	  policy pack, which stops on a mandatory violation (📖 R4.2.2). Prod runs allow no `--skip-preview`
356	  (📖 R4.1.2) and no targeting, replace, `state`, `import`, `destroy` (⚠️ R4.6 #3, G12). Pulumi Cloud,
357	  if used: OIDC via `pulumi/auth-actions`, no stored token (📖 R4.1.4).
358	- **Serverless v4:** `serverless package`; `serverless diff --json` (sf-core ≥ 4.37.0), parsed by CI
359	  because differences do not change the exit code (📖 R4.4.2); `serverless deploy --package`
360	  (📖 R4.4.3); a least-privilege `deploymentRole`, which cannot be removed later and is usable by
361	  anyone who may operate the stack (📖 R4.4.5), so JIT roles get no stack-operation rights.
362	- **State:** writable by deploy roles (and possibly the drift role, layer 7); Pulumi
363	  secrets via `awskms` on a DIY backend (📖 R4.3.3, R4.3.4; ⚠️ R4.6 #7).
364	- **k0s [design]:** manifests in the monorepo, applied by CI; no write RBAC for humans or agents in
365	  prod; read roles exclude logs and exec in namespaces with claim data (mechanism: G1). The risk
366	  stop is described for Pulumi and Serverless only; for k0s manifests (RBAC changes are the IAM
367	  equivalent) a `kubectl diff`-based stop is a candidate, not researched (⚠️ G1). Firebase deploys
368	  have no preview step in this design (⚠️ G2).
369	- **Incident lane:** label `incident`, on-call approver paged, security checks always run (S10), only
370	  slow unrelated tests skipped [design].
371	
372	**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)
373	
374	The incident responder is engineer E; the on-call approver is R (a backup replaces R only if R is
375	unavailable).
376	
377	1. E's incident-analysis session reads metrics and redacted logs and proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s,
378	   memory 1024 → 2048 MB, and a larger visibility timeout on the source queue (ratio ⚠️ Options §8).
379	2. A second session (edit tools; not meant to use prod roles) edits `serverless.yml`, runs
380	   `serverless diff` on non-prod, and opens a PR labelled `incident` as E.
381	3. R, a co-owner of `serverless.yml` through the on-call group (OD9), reviews the diff. If R
382	   catches a missing queue change, R does not fix it (OD7): E pushes the fix, the stale approval is
383	   dismissed, and R approves again, one more review round (Options §6). E merges.
384	4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, finds no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
385	5. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6) against ≤ 30 min: measured first in rollout.
386	
387	**Audit evidence.** The PR (diff, approvers, checks); run log and preview artifact, exported because
388	retention is unverified (⚠️ G7); deploy-role CloudTrail events; all linked by commit SHA and run ID.
389	
390	**Cost / value.** One approver for every prod change, from the owners of the path; two approvals by
391	the same approver when the risk stop fires. Cross-team PRs: open (OQ-A). None in non-prod.
392	Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub. Gap: on Team the prod diff is not seen before apply.

433	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
434	
435	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
436	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
437	checks as human code (S10).
438	
439	**On Papaya's stack**
440	
441	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
442	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
443	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
444	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
445	  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
446	  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
447	  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
448	  - stored only as an **environment secret of `production`**, never as a repository secret. Anyone
449	    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
450	    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
451	    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
452	    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
453	  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
454	    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be
455	    treated like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5). Self-hosted runners "can be persistently
456	    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which
457	    repositories use them (📖 R3.5.2); in a monorepo any workflow can likely target the runner's label (⚠️ G15).
458	    How to restrict a runner to one workflow is not researched (⚠️ G15); just-in-time runners exist
459	    (📖 R3.5.2, not read in detail). If reaching k0s needs a self-hosted runner, that
460	    runner is dedicated to the `production` deploy, and the residual risk is recorded;
461	  - that environment secret is the single source of truth: no copy elsewhere (OD1);
462	  - an owner, an expiry and rotation in the exception register;
463	  - optionally a separate environment (e.g. `production-k0s`), limited to `main` and referenced
464	    only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read these secrets
465	    [design].
466	
467	  Residual risk: admins can change the environment, and a deleted environment comes back without
468	  protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); the alerts and settings comparison in layer 7 cover this. The exception
469	  covers **CI deploy credentials only**. Runtime credentials, such as a k0s autoscaler's AWS access to

471	  role attached to the machine; ⚠️ not researched for k0s, G1).
